sentences.text: The name Eodromaeus combines the Greek words for 'dawn' and 'runner', while the species name 'murphi' honors Jim Murphy, who worked near the fossil discovery site.
This dinosaur possessed a low, rectangular skull approximately 12 centimeters long that featured an expansive antorbital fenestra edged below by a sharp ridge.

Its mouth contained fifteen knife-shaped teeth in the cranium, with the longest ones located in the front half of the upper jaw, and a row of tiny teeth was present on the pterygoid bone of the palate.
Eodromaeus reached a total length of about 1.2 meters and weighed between 4.5 and 6.8 kilograms.
Paul Sereno estimated that Eodromaeus could run at speeds of about 32 kilometers per hour.
Fossils of Eodromaeus were first discovered in 1996 by paleontologist Ricardo N. Martinez and volunteer Jim Murphy.
The genus Eodromaeus and its type species E. murphi were named in 2011 by a team including Ricardo N. Martinez and Paul C. Sereno.
Eodromaeus was a basal carnivorous theropod with forelimbs much shorter than its hindlimbs, ending in hands with five digits.
While the exact speed is unknown, it has been suggested that Eodromaeus could run at about 30 kilometers per hour.
Eodromaeus is classified within the order Saurischia.
Eodromaeus belongs to the suborder Theropoda.
Eodromaeus is considered one of the earliest members of Theropoda, the group that includes carnivorous dinosaurs.
The parent group of Eodromaeus is Saurischia.
Eodromaeus lived approximately 230 million years ago in the Carnian stage of the Late Triassic within the Ischigualasto Formation in northwestern Argentina.
All known specimens of Eodromaeus lived within the humid Scaphonyx-Exaeretodon-Herrerasaurus biozone in the Ischigualasto Formation.
When first described in 2011, Eodromaeus was considered the earliest member of the Theropoda.
A later study by Baron et al. (2017) placed Eodromaeus as a basal herrerasaurian and moved the family Herrerasauridae outside of Dinosauria.
This hypothesis has been questioned since then, with Bergman and Sues claiming Eoraptor as a theropod, like Eodromaeus.
